questions.question: A right prism-shaped planter box has a base with an area of 24 cm², and the box is 10 cm tall. Thinking of the prism as 10 identical layers stacked up, what is its volume?
questions.explain: For any right prism, volume = area of the base × height, so each 1 cm layer holds 24 cm³ and 10 layers hold 24 × 10 = 240 cm³. The common traps are adding 24 + 10 instead of multiplying, and labelling the answer in cm² — volume is always measured in cubic units.

questions.question: A cylindrical candle has a radius of 5 cm and a height of 4 cm. Using π ≈ 3.14, what is its volume?
questions.explain: Find the circle base first: π r² = 3.14 × 5 × 5 = 78.5 cm², then multiply by the height: 78.5 × 4 = 314 cm³. The most common mistake is using r instead of r² (3.14 × 5 × 4 = 62.8), or stopping at the base area of 78.5 and forgetting to multiply by the height.

questions.question: Noah packs soup in a rectangular container that measures 10 cm long, 6 cm wide and 5 cm deep. If he fills it right to the top, how much soup does it hold?
questions.explain: Volume = 10 × 6 × 5 = 300 cm³, and since 1 cm³ = 1 mL, the container holds 300 mL. Watch two traps: adding the three dimensions instead of multiplying, and mixing up mL with L — 300 mL is only a small bowl, while 300 L would fill a bathtub.

questions.question: In science class there are two containers, both 12 cm tall. One is a cylinder with a base area of 50 cm²; the other is a rectangular prism, also with a base area of 50 cm². Which one holds more?
options: The cylinder, because round containers hold more
The rectangular prism, because its base has straight sides
There is not enough information until you know the radius
They hold exactly the same: 600 cm³ each
questions.explain: Every right prism, round or straight-sided, has volume = base area × height, so 50 × 12 = 600 cm³ for both. The trap is thinking the shape of the base matters on its own — only its area and the height do, so the radius is not needed once you already know the base area.

questions.question: A can of soup from the food drive has a diameter of 8 cm and a height of 10 cm. Using π ≈ 3.14, what is the volume of the can?
questions.explain: The diameter is 8 cm, so the radius is 4 cm: base area = 3.14 × 4 × 4 = 50.24 cm², then 50.24 × 10 = 502.4 cm³. The classic error here is putting the diameter straight into πr² (3.14 × 8 × 8 × 10 = 2009.6), which gives four times too much — always halve the diameter first.

questions.question: The classroom fish tank is a rectangular prism 40 cm long and 25 cm wide. Ava fills it with water to a depth of 20 cm. How many litres of water is that?
questions.explain: The water forms a prism: 40 × 25 × 20 = 20 000 cm³ = 20 000 mL, and 1000 mL = 1 L, so it is 20 L. The most common slip is skipping the conversion and answering 20 000 L — check whether the number makes sense, since 20 000 L would be a swimming pool.

questions.question: Before the soccer game, the coach fills a cylindrical jug with water to a depth of 40 cm; the jug has a radius of 10 cm. Each player's bottle holds 400 mL. Using π ≈ 3.14, how many bottles can be filled completely?
questions.explain: Volume = 3.14 × 10 × 10 × 40 = 12 560 cm³ = 12 560 mL, and 12 560 ÷ 400 = 31.4, so only 31 bottles can be filled right up. Two traps: forgetting to square the radius (which gives about 3 bottles), and rounding 31.4 up to 32 — the leftover 0.4 is not a full bottle.

questions.question: Two cylindrical candles are both 10 cm tall. The small one has a radius of 3 cm; the large one has a radius of 6 cm. How much more wax does the large candle need?
options: Twice as much, because the radius doubled
questions.explain: Doubling the radius multiplies the base area by 2² = 4 (from 3.14 × 9 = 28.26 cm² to 3.14 × 36 = 113.04 cm²), and with the same height the volume is 4 times as big: 282.6 cm³ versus 1130.4 cm³. The big misconception in this unit is assuming double the radius means double the volume — the radius gets squared, so its effect is much stronger.
